episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Monday, March 16, 2026. Here's what's happening in A.I. and higher education.
-
Today, faculty at a Denver university say online assessments can no longer be validated in the A.I. age, and schools nationwide are flipping their classrooms to adapt.
-
In Insights and Trends today, Metropolitan State University Denver is confronting a fundamental challenge with student assessment as artificial intelligence tools become more capable.

According to Denver 7, faculty members say online testing has become nearly impossible to validate. Jeff Loats, professor and director of the Center for Teaching, Learning and Design at MSU Denver, stated that if assessments are online, quote, we don't know how to do that in a valid way, end quote.

Sam Jay, Executive Director of Online Learning at MSU, described this moment as an opportunity to, quote, right the ship, end quote, on assessment practices that have been in place for years. Vice Provost Shaun Schafer has already made dramatic changes to his journalism class, flipping the traditional model entirely. He has moved from in-person lectures with online assignments to online lectures with in-person assignments.

Schafer anticipates more case studies and assignments asking students to apply concepts to their own lives and communities, because these types of assignments are harder for A.I. to complete authentically. The focus is shifting from knowledge recall to knowledge application.

Faculty buy-in varies considerably across the institution. Some professors allow limited A.I. use while others restrict it entirely, creating a patchwork approach across departments. With more than one hundred majors at MSU Denver, creating definitive university-wide guidelines remains an evolving challenge. Each discipline faces different considerations depending on the nature of their assessments.
-
In Case Studies, Universidad Austral in Argentina has partnered with Universidad de La Sabana in Colombia to develop an intelligent dashboard for student assessment.

According to Times Higher Education, the tool allows educators and students to interact with A.I. as both teammate and teaching assistant. The system provides continuous feedback throughout the learning process and helps students develop better judgment in when and how to use A.I. appropriately. The international partnership demonstrates how institutions across borders are collaborating on A.I. integration solutions for higher education. Both universities are tracking outcomes to measure the dashboard's effectiveness in improving student performance.
-
Turning to Practical Tips, the San Diego Community College District is hosting an event called InnovAItion Day on Thursday, March 20.

According to City Times, the event brings together faculty, staff, and students across the district's campuses to explore responsible A.I. use in education. Student-led panels will feature discussions about A.I.'s role in learning from the perspective of those most affected by classroom A.I. policies. The district is using this event as an opportunity for cross-campus conversation about A.I. policies, best practices, and shared concerns. Registration is open to all members of the San Diego Community College District community.
-
In another Case Study, the University of North Carolina Greensboro's School of Nursing has appointed A.I. Champions to lead integration efforts across the program.

According to UNC Greensboro, these faculty members are integrating artificial intelligence across curriculum design, clinical simulation, and faculty training. Seventy percent of nursing faculty are now actively using A.I. tools to enhance student engagement and support different learning styles in the program. The A.I. Champions serve as resources for colleagues navigating questions about integration, from technical implementation to pedagogical considerations. The School of Nursing is documenting its approach as a potential model for other health science programs.
-
Also in Case Studies, George Washington University Professor Michael Tadesse has fundamentally restructured his marketing courses around what he calls an innovation mindset lab.

According to GW Today, students in the lab work directly with real businesses to build A.I.-enabled prototypes that address actual market challenges. Tadesse's approach emphasizes strategic thinking and professional adaptation over traditional content delivery and memorization. Students learn to evaluate A.I. tools critically, selecting the right technology for specific business problems. The lab model provides hands-on experience with A.I. in a business context while developing skills that transfer across industries.
-
In Practical Tips, new analysis examines how no-code A.I. platforms are expanding access for academic users without technical backgrounds.

According to Open Source For You, these tools enable students and faculty to leverage artificial intelligence without programming expertise or coding knowledge. Options range from beginner-friendly platforms for image recognition projects to sophisticated research assistants designed specifically for literature review and academic research. The accessibility of these no-code tools is lowering barriers to A.I. adoption across disciplines, from humanities departments to business schools. Faculty who previously avoided A.I. due to technical requirements can now incorporate these capabilities into their courses.
-
That's today's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.
